items.title: Build
items.text:
Build prepares small molecules and proteins already imported into the project. Open it from the left tool rail, choose a molecule type, and enable the operations you want to run. The central Molecules table shows the scope being prepared; table filters and the global ligand or receptor selection narrow that scope.

Use Build to change molecular structures before docking or other analyses. Program-specific docking preparation is configured separately in Docking Studio.

items.title: 1. Choose the molecules
items.text:
Select Small molecules or Proteins. The Molecules table switches to that type, and the action bar summarizes the number of molecules in scope. Review that count before starting a run.

For a project with a screening library, Ligands from lets you choose project rows, screening shards, or both. Conformer ensembles apply to project rows; they are not generated for molecules kept in shards.

items.title: 2. Prepare small molecules
items.text: Tick the sections to include in the build. Enabled operations run in this order: protonation, 3D generation, conformer generation, then minimization. Minimization is displayed before the conformer controls in the panel, but runs after conformer generation when both are enabled.

items.title: Protonation
items.text:
Choose a method and, for methods that predict protonation states, a pH:

  • Dimorphite-DL assigns a single pH-dependent state using protonation rules.
  • OpenBabel performs pH-dependent protonation through its command-line tool.
  • pKasso selects the most probable state at the chosen pH. Choose MolGpKa (fast) or MolGpKa + Uni-pKa (precise), set the thread count, and optionally request a GPU for the mixed model.
  • Explicit Hs (RDKit) adds hydrogens while preserving the current charge states. The pH control is disabled for this method.

These operations retain one state per molecule rather than adding separate records for alternative protonation microstates. OpenBabel and pKasso report their runtime availability in the panel; install missing runtimes through Settings → External tools.

items.title: 3D generation
items.text: Choose ETKDGv3 or srETKDGv3 (small rings) and set Attempts. Missing hydrogens are added during embedding. With multiple attempts, each candidate is optimized using MMFF, with UFF as a fallback, and the lowest-energy candidate is retained.

items.title: Conformer ensemble
items.text: Set Num conformers and Prune RMS to generate an ensemble and remove similar conformers. This step uses the random seed from Advanced. If Minimization is also enabled, it applies to every conformer, with another pruning pass after optimization.

items.title: Minimization
items.text: Choose MMFF or UFF and set Max iterations. Enable this section when you want geometry optimization as part of the build, including optimization of a conformer ensemble.

items.title: 3. Prepare proteins
items.text: In the Proteins tab, enable the operations needed for the structures in scope. The run performs them in the following order.

items.title: 3D generation
items.text:
In the receptors tab, users can import one or more sequences in fasta format using the Add sequence button or import from Uniprot using Download.

Users can then predict a structure from its sequence using ESMFold2 fast or ESMFold2 models. The ESMFold2 fast option is a faster, lower-accuracy version of the full ESMFold2 model. The ESMFold2 option uses the full model for higher accuracy predictions. This optional step uses an external service and requires an API token, entered through API token.... Enable Force: predict again proteins that already have 3D to replace an existing model with a new prediction. Below are the steps to obtain an API token from Biohub.ai:

  1. Open Biohub Developer Console and choose Sign up to create a free account or Log in if you already have one.

  2. After signing in, enter a descriptive API Key Name, such as AMDockVS, and select Create. Copy the generated API token.

  3. In AMDockVS, open Build → Proteins → 3D generation → API token..., paste the token, and select OK. Leave Remember unchecked to use it only for the current session. Enable Remember to save it in your shell profile (or user environment on Windows) for future sessions.

Having a valid API token, we can now predict the 3D structure of a protein from its sequence. Select ESMFold2 fast or ESMFold2 and click Run to start the prediction. The predicted structure will be added to the Molecules table once the process is complete.

items.title: Fix structure
items.text: Choose Current to work from the latest successful structure or Original to start from the imported structure. The repair options can add missing residues and atoms, replace nonstandard residues, and remove heterogens. Keep water when removing heterogens controls whether waters survive that removal. Structure repair requires PDBFixer and OpenMM. Use Open External tools… to install them from Settings → External tools → Protein preparation. Installing PDBFixer also installs OpenMM. Build detects the installed packages without restarting the application.

items.title: Protonation
items.text: Choose Reduce or PDB2PQR. The pH and Forcefield controls apply to PDB2PQR, with AMBER, CHARMM, and PARSE available as forcefields. Install the selected tool with Open External tools…, or from Settings → External tools → Protein preparation. Reduce and PDB2PQR use separate managed environments; Build detects them after installation without an application restart. AMDockVS requires Reduce 4.15 or PDB2PQR 3.7.1 for the respective method and does not automatically use copies found on the system PATH. PDB2PQR uses PROPKA to apply the selected pH. Reduce optimizes hydrogen placement without a pH control.

items.title: Minimization
items.text: Protein minimization uses OpenMM, available from Settings → External tools → Protein preparation or the section's Open External tools… button. Choose the forcefield files, then set Max iterations and Tolerance (kJ/mol/nm). This operation is optional and is off by default.

items.title: 4. Run and review
items.text:
Under Advanced, set the batch size and, when multiple destinations are available, Run on. Small-molecule builds also expose a Random seed. Select Run to submit the enabled operations and follow their progress in the action bar or Jobs monitor. Save to workflow records the configured operations for reuse.

After completion, select a molecule in the central table to inspect its current structure in PyMOL. Review any reported build failures before continuing to Docking Studio.

items.title: Where your data lives
items.text: A project is one folder. Molecules, prepared inputs and docked poses are not separate files in it: their bytes sit in a few large append-only files, and the database keeps a reference to each one. A project of 700,000 docked molecules is still a few dozen files, so it copies, backs up and syncs like a small one.

items.title: The project folder
items.text:
Path What it holds project.db The SQLite database: every molecule, set, binding site, result and interaction, plus the index of the structures. volumes/ The structures themselves: imported molecules, receptors, prepared PDBQT, poses, references. Files of up to 1 GB, named 000000001.vol, 000000002.vol... executor.db The job journal. An interrupted job resumes from it. config.toml Project settings. logs/ The project log. shards/ HTPVS ligand libraries (Parquet shards). docking/ Result fragments of sharded campaigns, and the docking programs' working files. models/ QSAR models. pockets/ P2Rank outputs; the viewer draws pocket points from them. clustering_runs/ The plot data of each diversity clustering run. cache/ Files rebuilt on demand (a structure written out for a viewer, docking inputs, a 2D diagram). Safe to delete. tmp/ Job temporaries, removed when the job ends.

A new project holds only the databases, config.toml and logs/: every other folder appears the first time something is written there. Exports go wherever you choose in the save dialog, which opens in the folder of the previous export.

Copy or move the whole folder. Never copy project.db without volumes/: the database only points at the structures.

items.title: Keeping storage tidy
items.text:
Deleting molecules or results, or re-docking, leaves the old bytes in the volumes until they are compacted. Click the project name in the status bar to open the project summary. Its Structure storage section shows the size and the share of dead bytes:

  • Check reads every structure and reports anything missing or damaged.
  • Compact rewrites the volumes that are mostly dead bytes and frees the space.

When a project opens, AMDockVS runs a fast check in the background and posts a notice to the bell only if something needs a repair. When the last job ends, it compacts the volumes that are more than half dead bytes on its own.

A script does not get that automatic step. From Python:

level, title, text = runtime.check_storage()   # fast check: ("info" | "warning" | "error", ...)
runtime.compact_storage_if_due()               # compacts when no job runs; None if nothing was due

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
Since structures are not files, getting them out is an export. Right-click rows in a table:

  • Ligands / Receptors → Export structures (ZIP)...: one file per molecule, in its own format (.sdf, .pdb, .cif...), named after the molecule.
  • Results → Export poses (SDF)...: one SDF with the selected poses. Each pose carries its ligand, receptor, engine, protocol and score, and its RMSD, ligand efficiency and predicted pKi when known, as SDF data fields.
  • Results → Export poses (ZIP)...: one file per pose, as the engine wrote it.

From Python, the same functions the menus use:

from amdockvs.core.payloads import payload_store
from amdockvs.io.export import export_poses_sdf, export_structures

store = payload_store(runtime)
hits = runtime.docking.top_hits(limit=100)
export_poses_sdf(store, hits, "top100.sdf")
export_structures(store, [(hit.ligand_name, hit.pose_payload_id) for hit in hits], "top100.zip")

export_structures writes a ZIP when the destination ends in .zip, otherwise a folder. Both return how many structures were written.

To read one structure in a script, use read_structure(runtime, payload_id) from amdockvs.core.payloads. It returns the text and its format.

items.title: Diversity
items.text:
Diversity groups ligands by molecular similarity and lets you choose representatives from the resulting clusters. Open it from the left tool rail to configure a run. Completed runs are reviewed in the separate Clusters view, opened from the top catalog or through Show clusters.

Clustering records a result without automatically changing the global ligand selection or excluding compounds. Those actions are available after you review the clusters.

items.title: 1. Choose the ligands
items.text:
Use Selection to choose All ligands, Current selection, a usage class (General, Reference, or General + Reference), or a saved set. When the project has a sharded screening library, Screening library (shards) is also available.

Current selection uses the global ligand selection made with right-click → Select in a ligand table. Other choices use their own scope and ignore that selection. For project rows, the Ligands table shows the chosen scope while the tool is open, and its column filters can narrow it further.

Only with can restrict project ligands to those with a value for an activity endpoint. Leave it at Any ligand when activity measurements are not required for your clustering run.

items.title: 2. Configure similarity and clustering
items.text:
Choose a Method (currently BitBIRCH) and set its Threshold in Method options. Higher thresholds produce tighter clusters and generally retain more clusters. Some methods also expose a batch-size control.

Under Morgan FP, set the fingerprint radius and nbits. The initial values are radius 2 and 2048 bits. The fingerprint settings affect similarity, so evaluate the clustering threshold together with those settings.

items.title: 3. Preview a sample
items.text:
Preview sample clusters a random sample to help you adjust the method and threshold before submitting a full run. It displays a two-dimensional projection in the Distribution panel. Repeated previews accumulate samples; once all molecules in the scope have been previewed, another click restores the existing plot. Changing the method, threshold, or other method options starts a fresh preview with the new settings. Clear resets the accumulated preview when you want to start again with the same settings.

Size distribution replaces the scatter plot with a histogram of compounds per cluster. Use it to see whether the preview contains many singletons or a few large clusters. Select Cluster plot to return to the accumulated scatter plot without taking another sample or clustering again. Previewing does not change molecule selection or exclusion state, and it does not replace a full clustering run.

items.title: 4. Cluster the full scope
items.text:
Select Cluster. AMDockVS counts the molecules and suggests a CPU count; accept or adjust that count to submit the clustering job. Follow the job in the Jobs monitor. The completed run opens in Clusters, where its scope, clusters, and representative molecules can be reviewed.

For a sharded screening library, clustering works on the library in its shards; its representatives become project ligand rows.

items.title: 5. Choose representatives
items.text:
In Clusters, select a run and review the representative row or an individual cluster to see its ligands. The Representatives controls let you change the selection strategy:

  • Centroid chooses members closest to the cluster centroid.
  • Medoid chooses members most similar, on average, to the rest of the cluster.
  • Extremes chooses members spanning the low, middle, and high values of the selected ranking.
  • Quartiles samples across quartiles of that ranking.
  • Proportional allocates representatives according to cluster size.

For strategies that use Rank by, choose similarity to the centroid or an available activity endpoint. Select Apply to update the representatives for that run.

items.title: 6. Use the result
items.text:
• Use as selection makes the ligands currently listed in the result view the global ligand selection, ready for tools such as Docking Studio.
  • Save as set... stores the run's representatives as a named ligand set.
  • Exclude non-representatives marks the other ligands of the run as excluded while retaining their records in the project.
  • Size distribution plots the cluster-size distribution for the run.
  • Cluster plot returns to the run's scatter plot, keeping the selected cluster and using the existing results without rerunning clustering.
  • Delete run removes the saved clustering run; it is separate from excluding molecules.

If the result is too large for a table selection, save the representatives as a set or use the exclusion action instead.

Continue with Docking Studio to dock a selected subset, or QSAR to model ligands with activity measurements.

items.title: Docking Studio
items.text: Docking Studio guides a docking run through four revisitable steps. In the first step Programs, users select the docking programs and settings. In second and third steps (Ligands and Receptors), users prepare the ligands and receptors for docking. The fourth step Preview & Run checks preparation and docking readiness before submitting work.

items.title: Typical workflow
items.text:
1. 01 Programs Select docking engines and settings
  2. 02 Ligands Prepare compound(s)
  3. 03 Receptors Prepare receptor(s) and define search space(s)
  4. 04 Preview & Run Check and launch
↳Docking ResultsScores · poses · interactions

You can return to any setup step to adjust its settings.

items.title: 1. Choose programs
items.text:
In this section, the users set the docking mode, select the docking programs to use, and configure program-specific settings. The docking mode can be either Docking or Redocking. In Docking mode, the selected programs will perform docking runs on the provided ligands and receptors. In Redocking mode, users can validate the docking protocols by attempting to reproduce known binding poses of ligands in their respective receptors. This is useful for validation purposes, as it allows users to assess the accuracy and reliability of the docking programs and settings they have chosen.

Available programs include AutoDock Vina, QuickVina 2, gnina, AutoDock-GPU and Uni-Dock. Program-specific settings appear when you select a program. The user can choose to run more than one program in parallel, and the docking results will be organized by program in the results view.

items.title: 2. Prepare ligands
items.text:
This step uses the ligand scope shown in the Ligands catalog; it does not have a separate table or scope selector. Select a preparation target to see its options. General Options includes Force re-prepare; the other entries correspond to preparation families shared by the selected docking programs.

If the project contains a sharded screening library, choose whether to prepare ligand rows, shards, or both under Ligands from. Advanced settings include preparation batch size and, when available, the execution destination. Select Prepare Ligands to submit preparation jobs and follow their progress in the Jobs monitor.

items.title: 3. Prepare receptors
items.text: The Receptors catalog supplies the scope for this step. Select a receptor there to inspect or change its active search box and grid settings. The Receptor preparation section has general options and options for the preparation families used by the selected programs. Force re-prepare, batch size and the execution destination are available here. Select Prepare Receptors to submit the preparation jobs.

items.title: 4. Preview and Run
items.text:
Review prepared ligand and receptor counts and the estimated docking tasks. A receptor must be prepared and have a search box before it is ready, otherwise it is skipped during docking. If preparation remains, Run Docking waits for the required preparation jobs to finish before submitting docking.

Skip pairs already docked is on by default; turn it off to run those receptor-ligand pairs again and replace their previous results. Compute interactions analyzes each pose after docking and stores the interaction data with the results. Advanced settings include docking batch size and, when available, the execution destination.

items.title: One configuration per program
items.text:
A project keeps a single docking configuration per program, so the results of a program are all comparable with each other. Redocking is the exception: it may hold several protocols, since comparing them is the point.

Changing a program's search settings once it already has docking results stops the run rather than mixing two kinds of result together, and offers to replace that program's results or to cancel. What counts as a change is the search itself — scoring function, exhaustiveness, seed, energy range, minimum RMSD, grid spacing, and a non-standard method. The number of poses kept (num_modes) does not: it says how many poses of the same search are stored, so asking for more poses later is a redock of the same protocol.

Replacing deletes that program's docking results in the project — poses, the analyses derived from them, the counters, and the per-shard result files — and does it after the request is checked but before the new run is submitted. A new run that then fails or is cancelled does not bring the deleted results back. Redocking results, other programs' results and the prepared ligand library are left alone. Through the API the same situation raises DockingProtocolConflictError, and replace_existing=True is the confirmation.

For a sharded screening library, Screening hits sets the score threshold and the maximum number of hits retained per receptor. Optional off-target docking first screens against a reference receptor, then docks the selected hits against the other ready receptors.

items.title: 5. Review results
items.text: After submission, Docking Studio opens Docking Results automatically. The main results table organizes poses by receptor, ligand and pose; additional tables provide off-target comparisons and redocking results when those data are available. Select a pose to inspect its score and structure, and view interaction diagrams when interaction analysis was computed.

items.title: Import, prepare, and dock
items.text:
This example mirrors the supported asynchronous workflow. Replace the input paths and box coordinates with values for your system. It docks with QuickVina 2: install it once with runtime.tools.install("qvina"), or leave out program and engine_config to dock with AutoDock Vina.

from pathlib import Path

from amdockvs import AMDockVSRuntime

runtime = AMDockVSRuntime()
try:
    runtime.create_or_open_project(
        name="quickstart",
        folder=Path("./quickstart-project"),
    )

    import_jobs = [
        *runtime.loader.load_ligands(["inputs/ligands.sdf"]),
        *runtime.loader.load_receptors(["inputs/receptor.pdb"]),
    ]
    runtime.watch_jobs(import_jobs)

    ligands = runtime.molecules.select(role="ligand")
    receptors = runtime.molecules.select(role="receptor")
    receptor = receptors.one()

    prep_jobs = [
        runtime.docking.prepare_ligands(ligands=ligands),
        runtime.docking.prepare_receptors(receptors=receptors),
    ]
    runtime.watch_jobs(prep_jobs)

    runtime.docking.set_grid(
        receptor_id=int(receptor.id),
        center=(12.0, 13.0, 10.0),
        size=(20.0, 20.0, 20.0),
    )
    job_id = runtime.docking.run(
        program="qvina",
        ligands=ligands,
        receptors=receptors,
        engine_config={"exhaustiveness": 8, "vina_cpu": 1},
    )
    runtime.watch_job(job_id)

    print(runtime.docking.result_stats())
finally:
    runtime.shutdown()

items.title: Notebook-friendly waiting
items.text:
Several chemistry methods accept wait=True when a blocking call is clearer:

status = runtime.chemistry.standardize_ligands(
    ligands=runtime.molecules.select(role="ligand"),
    wait=True,
)
print(status.status)

The API guide has an example for every part of the runtime.

items.title: Filter
items.text: Filter applies property rules to small-molecule records in the project. Use it to exclude molecules that fail your criteria, recover molecules previously excluded by this filter, or save matching molecules as a set. Open the tool from the left rail; the central Molecules table follows the source configured in the panel.

items.title: 1. Choose the source
items.text:
Under Source, select Small Molecules as the Molecule Type. The other listed types—proteins, peptides, nucleotides, and polymers—do not yet have filter criteria in this panel.

Choose a Target:

  • Outside Sets — Molecules that do not belong to a set.
  • Inside Sets — Molecules belonging to sets.
  • All Molecules — Include molecules regardless of set membership.
  • Specific Set — Choose one saved set from the Set list.

Usage further restricts the source to General, Reference, Derived, General + Reference, or All. The panel's Target and Usage controls define the filter source; review them before applying an action.

items.title: 2. Choose an action
items.text:
• Enrich - exclude failing molecules evaluates active molecules and marks those that fail as excluded. The records remain in the project.
  • Recover - re-include filter-excluded that now pass evaluates excluded molecules and restores those that pass the new criteria. It only recovers exclusions made by this Filter tool; exclusions made manually or by other tools remain in place.
  • Tag matches to a set (no state change) saves matching active molecules into the named set without changing their exclusion state. Enter the name under Tag into set.

items.title: 3. Add criteria
items.text:
Select Add Rule, choose a property and comparison operator, and enter its value when required. Add more rows to combine criteria; a molecule must pass every rule. Use Remove beside a row to discard it.

Available numeric properties include molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, fragment count, total and aromatic ring counts, heteroatom and heavy-atom counts, formal charge, fraction Csp3, and total atom count. Numeric rules support <, <=, >, >=, and =.

PAINS Matches and Ro5 Violations use is empty or has any. For example, PAINS Matches → is empty keeps molecules with no detected PAINS matches. Ro5 Violations → is empty requires no recorded Rule of 5 violations.

For a molecular-weight interval, add two rules, such as MW (Da) >= 200 and MW (Da) <= 500. These are example bounds; choose limits appropriate to your compound collection.

items.title: 4. Review counts and apply
items.text:
Select Apply Filter, or Tag to Set for the tagging action. AMDockVS evaluates the source and reports the counts before asking whether to apply the changes. Canceling that confirmation leaves the counts visible without changing the molecules.

Molecules missing properties required by the rules are reported as skipped. If a PAINS rule requires results that have not been calculated, the tool can offer to calculate PAINS matches before you try the filter again.

After applying, review the summary and open the Ligands catalog to inspect the resulting scope or saved set. You can use a saved set as input to Diversity or select its members for Docking Studio.

items.title: 2D Interactions
items.text:
2D Interactions displays a protein-ligand contact diagram for the pose selected in Docking Results. Open the panel from the right tool rail. It appears below PyMOL so that the diagram and the 3D complex can be inspected together.

The panel follows docking poses. Selecting an undocked ligand in the Ligands catalog does not create a contact diagram.

items.title: 1. Select a docking pose
items.text: Open Docking Results, select the receptor and ligand, then choose a pose in the pose table.

items.title: 2. Build the diagram
items.text:
Choose Build diagram in the selected result's Interactions section, or in the 2D panel's empty-state prompt. AMDockVS detects the contacts, calculates their diagram layout, and saves the result with that pose.

The screenshot shows the starting point for a pose without a computed diagram. Once calculation finishes, the 2D panel opens automatically with the contact map and reports the ligand name, pose number, and interaction count.

To analyze poses as docking finishes, enable Compute interactions in Docking Studio → Preview & Run. This populates the stored contact data. If a pose has no saved diagram layout, use Build diagram when reviewing it.

items.title: 3. Read contacts alongside the 3D structure
items.text:
The contact map places the ligand and interacting residues in a 2D layout. Use its legend to identify the interaction types and compare the diagram with the selected complex in PyMOL.

Select a residue in the diagram to inspect it in the 3D viewer. You can also select a row in the result's interaction table to display that individual contact in PyMOL. This makes it possible to check a contact's position in the structure as well as its reported type and distance.

items.title: 4. Adjust the diagram layout
items.text:
The diagram is fully interactive, click on the three dots in the top right corner of the panel to open it in a window and access all the controls:

  • Scroll to zoom and drag with the middle mouse button to pan.
  • Drag a residue to reposition it in the layout.
  • Use ↺ and ↻ to rotate the selected element; Mirror changes the ligand's diagram orientation.
  • Settle neighbors adjusts the rest of the layout after rotating an element.
  • Reshuffle generates another arrangement, and Recalculate rebuilds the layout.
  • Fit fits the diagram to the panel again.

These controls edit the diagram layout; they do not move atoms in the saved docking pose. The toolbar also provides backbone, solvent-exposure, legend, and style controls.

items.title: 5. Set defaults and export
items.text:
Use Defaults... in the diagram's settings menu to open the application's MS-ContactMap settings. These configure the diagram's appearance, including glyphs, colors, and surface and exposure styling.

Choose Export SVG... to save the displayed diagram as a vector image. The export reflects the current arrangement, including manual layout adjustments. For a 3D image of the same pose, use PyMOL's export.

items.title: Jobs monitor
items.text: The Jobs monitor shows the background work submitted by the active project, including imports, molecule preparation, pocket prediction, clustering, QSAR, and docking. It opens in a separate window so you can inspect a run while continuing to use the project workspace.

items.title: 1. Open the monitor
items.text:
Select Jobs on the right side of the top toolbar, or click the jobs indicator in the status bar. Tools that provide a See details link can also open the monitor for you.

Opening the window focuses running work first, with waiting work as the fallback. An already selected running job stays selected. If filters would hide the active job, the monitor clears them to reveal it. You can then select another job to inspect its details.

Closing the window hides the monitor; jobs continue in the background. Reopen it from Jobs whenever you need to check progress.

items.title: 2. Find a job
items.text:
The header identifies the active project and summarizes its jobs by status. The list on the left puts active jobs first. Each entry shows the job name, status, executor, progress, and elapsed or estimated remaining time.

Use the controls above the list to narrow what is shown:

  • Search jobs... searches job names, IDs, statuses, and executor names.
  • All statuses filters the list to one of the statuses present in the project.
  • Clicking a host card shows the jobs assigned to that host's executors.
  • Clicking the executor name in a selected job's detail header filters the list to that executor.
  • The host or executor filter chip clears that filter when clicked.
  • Resync requests fresh job information and reloads the selected job's error details.

Search, status, and host or executor filters apply together. Clear the search and return to All statuses if you want to browse the full job list.

items.title: 3. Read the job status
items.text:
Select a job to display its details on the right. Its status indicates the stage it has reached:

  • Waiting — Submitted but not yet running.
  • Running — Work is being executed.
  • Completed — The job has finished successfully.
  • Completed with errors — The job finished but reported errors; inspect its failures before using the results.
  • Failed — The job could not finish successfully.
  • Canceled — Execution was stopped by a cancellation request.
  • Interrupted — Execution stopped before the job completed.

The detail header also identifies the executor and shows start and elapsed times.

items.title: 4. Follow progress and resource use
items.text:
The host cards at the top show CPU, memory, and, when available, GPU activity for the local computer and hosts used by active executors. These charts describe the host as a whole. Queue login nodes are identified separately and do not show resource charts.

For the selected job, the detail panel provides:

  • ETA — An estimate of the remaining time based on recent throughput. It shows calculating until enough information is available.
  • Progress — Completed work and the distribution of pending, running, done, and failed chunks.
  • Throughput — The rate at which chunks are processed.
  • Failures — Failed chunks and reported job errors.

A chunk is a unit of work submitted by a tool. Depending on the operation and batch size, it may contain one molecule or a batch, so the chunk count is not necessarily the molecule count.

The Chunks panel shows individual chunk states when those data are available for the current session. After reopening an older run, the totals and summary can still be available even when the individual cells are not.

items.title: Running
items.text: The Running tab lists tasks currently in progress, with their input, host, attempt number, elapsed time, and reported progress. When enough tasks are present, the monitor highlights those taking substantially longer than the median task time.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
The Errors tab groups failures by their message. Select a group to read its recorded error or traceback below the list. Hover over a group to see examples of affected inputs and their attempt numbers. If only part of a large failure list has been read, the panel reports the remaining count.

Use these details to identify the input or missing requirement that needs attention before submitting more work. Resync reloads the error details if you need an updated view.

items.title: Summary
items.text: The Summary tab collects the job ID, status, executor, timestamps, elapsed time, chunk counts, retries, throughput, and available memory and CPU/GPU usage measurements. Select copy beside the job key to copy its ID when reporting a problem.

items.title: 6. Cancel, resume, or move a job
items.text:
Select a job before using the actions in the header:

  • Cancel requests cancellation of an active job. The header reports whether the request was accepted or failed.
  • Resume continues a canceled or interrupted job on the executor where it ran. This button is available for those stopped states.
  • Move to lists the available destination executors for a job that can be continued. Moving an active job stops it first, then continues it on the selected executor. If continuation is unavailable, the menu reports that the job cannot be continued.

Action availability depends on the job's state and execution context. If an action fails, read the message beside the project title. Use the application's Executors window to start or stop executors.

items.title: 7. Return to the results
items.text: When a job finishes, return to the tool or result view that submitted it: for example, Docking Results, QSAR Analysis, or Clusters. For preparation and import jobs, inspect the updated records in the molecule catalogs.

items.title: Ligands
items.text: The Ligands catalog contains molecules imported into the active project. Choose Import Ligands... in the catalog, or use File → Import Ligands..., to open the import panel. From there, add files or download compounds, set a molecule type for each file, and choose whether small molecules should be stored as project rows or kept as a screening library on disk.

items.title: Add ligand files
items.text:
Use the toolbar beside the table to add inputs:

  • Add files — Select one or more molecule files. Supported inputs include SDF/SD, MOL/MDL, MOL2, PDB, PDBQT, CIF/mmCIF, SMILES, CSV/TSV/text tables, and FASTA files.
  • Add folder — Add supported files from a folder and its subfolders.
  • Add SMILES — Paste one SMILES per line, optionally followed by a molecule name. AMDockVS saves the input as a temporary .smi file for import.
  • Download — Retrieve compounds from PubChem by CID or name, ChEMBL by compound ID, the ChEMBL approved-drug collection, the latest eMolecules free catalog, or URLs such as ZINC22 tranche and vendor files.
  • Remove — Remove selected files from this pending import.

You can also drag files or folders onto the table. Duplicate paths are added only once. Downloaded files can be kept for reuse on a later import; temporary downloads are removed after import, and project downloads can be reviewed in Settings → Downloads.

items.title: Review the input table
items.text:
The table has one row per input file:

Column What it controls Name The displayed file or downloaded compound-set name. Type Choose Small molecule, Protein, Peptide, Nucleotide, or Polymer. New rows default to Small molecule. Format The file extension detected for the input. Path The source file location. As Reference Mark curated ligands, such as co-crystals or measured actives, as references. Reference files are imported as project rows and are not placed in screening shards. The Activity tab reads measurements only from files marked this way.

Click a Type cell to select its molecule type. Click anywhere in an As Reference cell to toggle that mark.

items.title: Choose where a screening library goes
items.text:
The Screening library: keep on disk as shards option is for large small-molecule collections. When enabled, molecules remain in files on disk instead of becoming one database row per molecule; docking hits are written to the project. Reference files and non-small-molecule types still import as rows. AMDockVS suggests sharding when the queued small-molecule count reaches its configured threshold.

A project can have one screening library. If a project already has ligand rows, new imports go to the project database. If it already has a sharded library, the option stays selected for additional screening files. Turn it off for a row-based import, and mark curated files As Reference to put them in the reference context.

items.title: Set import options
items.text: The tabs below the table apply to small-molecule inputs. They become available when at least one file is assigned the Small molecule type.

items.title: Filters
items.text:
All filters are optional and are off unless stated otherwise. The Max Rotatable Bonds field starts at 32; 0 means no limit. The other numeric limits use 0 for no limit.

  • Exclude PAINS matches — Remove molecules matching PAINS substructure patterns.
  • Require Rule of 5 compliance — Keep molecules with no more than the selected maximum number of Lipinski Rule of 5 violations. The default is no maximum.
  • Max Rotatable Bonds — Set the upper limit on rotatable bonds.
  • Max Heavy Atoms — Set the upper limit on heavy atoms.
  • MW range — Set a lower and/or upper molecular-weight bound.
  • Include SMARTS — Keep molecules matching every comma-separated SMARTS pattern.
  • Exclude SMARTS — Remove molecules matching any comma-separated SMARTS pattern.

items.title: Prepare
items.text:
Each preparation option is off by default and runs only when the corresponding feature is missing:

  • Add hydrogens (if missing) — Add explicit hydrogens when absent.
  • Generate 3D coordinates (if missing) — Generate a 3D conformer using ETKDG; this also adds hydrogens and can take time for very large libraries.
  • Standardize to canonical tautomer — Select one canonical tautomer per molecule. This does not enumerate tautomers as separate molecules.
  • Split fragments into separate molecules — Keep the largest organic fragment as the main molecule and import other distinct organic fragments as separate molecules; duplicate fragments and ions are skipped.

items.title: QSAR, Clustering and Diverse
items.text: These tabs are placeholders in the import panel. QSAR model filtering is not available during import. Clustering and diversity selection run after import; use Molecule Tools → Diversity for those operations.

items.title: Activity
items.text:
The Activity tab is enabled only when at least one input is marked As Reference. Enter an SDF property tag or table column under Activity from file tag/column. The optional endpoint name defaults to that tag; the unit can be selected or entered, and the transform can be left as (none) or set to pIC50, pKi, or pEC50.

For a reference CSV, TSV, text, or SMILES table, the panel detects numeric columns and offers them as checkboxes. Select the columns to import as activity endpoints. Columns containing only 0 and 1 are identified as categorical; other numeric columns are identified as continuous. Detected columns are not selected automatically.

items.title: Start the import
items.text: Add at least one file, review its type and reference status, and select Import. The options in the tabs apply to small-molecule files; other types are imported using their selected type. Reference small molecules are loaded as project rows, while non-reference small molecules can be sent to the screening shards when that option is selected. Follow the submitted work in the Jobs monitor; AMDockVS opens the Ligands catalog or the Shards view based on where the imported molecules are stored.

items.title: Main page
items.text: The main page appears when AMDockVS starts without an open project. The center of the window contains the project controls, while the tutorial card stays visible alongside them. From here, you can open an existing project, create a new one, or start the guided docking example.

items.title: Projects
items.text:
Select Open or Create Project... to open the AMDock projects dialog. It lists the projects registered with AMDockVS so you can choose one to open or create a new project. Use New project to enter a name and storage folder; you can also add tags and a description to help identify the project later. After you save, AMDockVS opens the new project in the workspace.

An AMDockVS project represents one docking study or screening campaign. It groups the molecule records, settings, jobs, and results for that work in one project folder. Its main files are:

  • project.db, a SQLite database containing molecule records, sets, binding sites, docking results, and interactions.
  • volumes/ stores structure data such as imported molecules, prepared inputs, and docking poses. The database keeps references to these structures.
  • executor.db records job state.
  • config.toml stores project-specific settings.

Folders for models, pockets, shards, and docking artifacts are added as those features are used. See Where your data lives for the full folder layout and backup guidance.

items.title: Tutorial
items.text: The Your first docking card starts an eight-step, hands-on walkthrough using the Vps34 receptor and SAR405 ligand. It guides you through creating a practice project, importing the example molecules, opening Docking Studio, choosing AutoDock Vina, preparing the ligand and receptor, defining the docking box, and launching the calculation. You perform each action in the application as the tutorial guides you through the workflow. The tutorial ends when the docking job is submitted; poses and scores appear in Docking Results after the calculation finishes.

items.title: Main page
items.text: The main page appears when AMDockVS starts without an open project. The center of the window contains the project controls, while the tutorial card stays visible alongside them. From here, you can open an existing project, create a new one, or start the guided docking example.

items.title: Projects
items.text:
Select Open or Create Project... to open the AMDock projects dialog. It lists the projects registered with AMDockVS so you can choose one to open or create a new project. Use New project to enter a name and storage folder; you can also add tags and a description to help identify the project later. After you save, AMDockVS opens the new project in the workspace.

An AMDockVS project represents one docking study or screening campaign. It groups the molecule records, settings, jobs, and results for that work in one project folder. Its main files are:

  • project.db, a SQLite database containing molecule records, sets, binding sites, docking results, and interactions.
  • volumes/ stores structure data such as imported molecules, prepared inputs, and docking poses. The database keeps references to these structures.
  • executor.db records job state.
  • config.toml stores project-specific settings.

Folders for models, pockets, shards, and docking artifacts are added as those features are used. See Where your data lives for the full folder layout and backup guidance.

items.title: Workspace
items.text:
AMDockVS opens projects in a dockable, multi-panel workspace. Each workspace contains three main areas:

  • The top catalog and result views in the center open as tabs (e.g., receptors and ligands tabs, docking results)
  • The left tool rail opens one task panel at a time (e.g., docking studio, QSAR)
  • The right tool rail open visualization panels (e.g., PyMOL, 2D contacts)

Next, we describe the tools and panels available in AMDockVS.

items.title: Top catalog
items.text:
• Receptors — Import one or more receptor structures from databases or local files.
  • Ligands — Import ligand files, set molecule types, and choose whether to store a screening library as shards.

items.title: Main analysis tools
items.text:
• Docking Studio — Configure docking programs, prepare molecules and launch runs.
  • QSAR — Build models from activity data and apply them to ligands or screening libraries.

items.title: Secondary analysis tools
items.text:
• Build — Prepare small molecules and proteins, including 3D conformer generation.
  • Pocket Detection — Predict potential binding sites.
  • Filter — Apply criteria to small-molecule records.
  • Diversity — Cluster compounds by molecular similarity and choose representatives.

items.title: Visualization tools
items.text:
• PyMOL — Visualize molecules and their interactions in 3D.
  • 2D Interactions — Inspect molecular interactions in 2D diagrams.

items.title: Job monitoring
items.text: • Jobs monitor — Follow background jobs, inspect progress and errors, and cancel, resume, or move work between executors.

items.title: Pocket Detection
items.text: Pocket Detection runs P2Rank on receptor structures and stores the predicted binding sites in the project. Open it from the left tool rail. The Receptors catalog supplies the structures to process, and the Binding Sites view shows the predictions for the receptor you are inspecting.

items.title: 1. Choose receptors
items.text:
The run uses the current receptor-table scope, including table filters and the global receptor selection. The Scope line in the tool shows how many receptors will be processed.

Exclude receptors with defined ligands is checked by default. It hides receptors whose import metadata already contains reference ligands. Clear this option to predict pockets for those receptors as well. If the resulting scope is empty, adjust this option or the filters in the Receptors catalog.

items.title: 2. Set prediction options
items.text:
• Profile — Choose Ignore B-factors (predicted models, NMR, cryo-EM) (the default) or Use B-factors (X-ray structures). The selected profile applies to the whole run, including runs containing a mixture of structure types.
  • Threads — Set the number of CPU threads used by P2Rank.

Ignore B-factors (predicted models, NMR, cryo-EM) is AMDockVS's default. It uses P2Rank's AlphaFold prediction model, which keeps the chemical and geometric features but omits B-factors. Keep this option when B-factors are missing, uncertain, or contain prediction confidence scores. It also provides a fallback for mixed collections whose B-factor provenance is uncertain. P2Rank recommends this model for AlphaFold models and NMR or cryo-EM structures. For example, AlphaFold PDB files store pLDDT confidence scores in the B-factor field; these values have a different meaning from experimental X-ray B-factors.

The B-factor-free profile also uses its own score-to-probability calibration. Changing profiles can therefore change the predicted pockets, their ranking, scores, and probabilities for the same receptor coordinates.

Use B-factors (X-ray structures) uses P2Rank's standard prediction model, which combines chemical and geometric features of the protein surface with atomic B-factors. Choose this profile for X-ray crystal structures with meaningful experimental B-factors.

The differences between the two profiles are defined in P2Rank's Standard and AlphaFold configurations.

P2Rank and Java 17 or later must be available. When the runtime is missing, the P2Rank Runtime section reports its status and provides Open Settings to reach Settings → External tools.

Running another profile replaces the current predictions for the receptors in scope after the new calculation succeeds. Review or record the sites you need before submitting a replacement run.

items.title: 3. Run P2Rank
items.text:
Select Run P2Rank. While prediction is running, the status line reports progress and See details opens the Jobs monitor. The tool prevents another prediction run from being submitted while its current work is active.

When the job finishes, select a receptor in the Receptors catalog to inspect its predicted sites in the Binding Sites view.

items.title: 4. Inspect predicted sites
items.text:
The results table lists the binding-site ID (BS), rank, score, probability, profile, box center, box size, and pocket residues. The Score cells use the same colors as the pockets in PyMOL: violet for lower scores and yellow for higher scores within that receptor's predictions.

Select one or more site rows to display their pocket points and centers on the receptor in PyMOL. The binding-site presets there let you switch between points, nearby residues, and a local surface.

items.title: 5. Use a site for docking
items.text:
Select the site you want and choose Use as Active Docking Site. This makes that site's box the active docking search space for the receptor. Selecting rows to visualize pockets does not activate them for docking by itself.

Review the box in PyMOL's Grid Box panel or in Docking Studio → Receptors, adjust it if needed, and prepare the receptor before launching docking.

items.title: PyMOL
items.text: PyMOL is the embedded 3D viewer on the right side of the workspace. It shows receptor structures, ligands, docking poses, and binding-site boxes. Open it from the right tool rail, then select a molecule or docking pose in the central catalog to inspect it.

items.title: 1. Choose what to display
items.text:
The viewer follows the structure selected in the active catalog or result view. Select a receptor to inspect its structure and active binding site, a ligand to inspect that molecule, or a pose in Docking Results to see the receptor–ligand complex.

In Pocket Detection, selecting predicted sites displays their pocket points and centers on the receptor. The available display presets change with the kind of scene being shown.

PyMOL displays the coordinates stored for the selected molecule. To generate a 3D structure or change its preparation, use Build or Docking Studio.

For an ESMFold prediction, open the bottom Panel and choose Color by pLDDT. The prediction and confidence data remain saved when you reopen the project. After structure preparation, Color prediction by pLDDT displays the saved prediction with its original confidence values; Show Current returns to the prepared working structure.

items.title: 2. Use the viewer toolbar
items.text:
The toolbar provides the following actions. In a narrow panel, some actions move into its overflow menu.

  • Selection — Choose whether mouse picks select atoms, residues, chains, or objects. The menu also clears the PyMOL selection.
  • Actions — Use Zoom, Orient, or Center on the current PyMOL selection or scene target.
  • Display — Apply Cartoon, Sticks, Lines, Surface, Spheres, Ribbon, or Dots. In comparison scenes, the menu also offers Grid and Overlay layouts.
  • Hide — Hide a representation or everything for the current selection or scene target.
  • Hydrogens — Show polar hydrogens (bonded to N, O, or S) by default. Click to cycle through hidden, all, and polar hydrogens in the PyMOL session.
  • Presets — Apply a display preset compatible with the current scene.

The atom or residue selection made inside PyMOL controls viewer actions. The global molecule selection used by Build and Docking Studio is made separately in the catalog tables.

items.title: 3. Choose a display preset
items.text:
AMDockVS adds presets for the main kinds of scene:

  • AMDock · Receptor shows the receptor as a cartoon with atom coloring based on its role.
  • AMDock · Ligand centers the ligand and shows it as sticks.
  • AMDock · Protein-ligand shows the protein as a cartoon and the ligand or docking pose as sticks.
  • Binding sites · Points, Binding sites · Residues, and Binding sites · Surface show different views of a predicted pocket.
  • Surface · Site highlight and Surface · Residue nature show the search-space region on a receptor surface, using either a highlight color or residue chemical properties.

The menu only offers presets that apply to the current scene. Select a predicted pocket first to use its binding-site presets.

items.title: 4. Inspect the search space
items.text:
Grid Box opens the side panel beside the 3D canvas. Select a receptor to review its sites and the center and dimensions of its working box. The panel's save and activation actions control which site is used for docking.

Use Pocket Detection to predict candidate sites, or review the receptor's active box during the Receptors step of Docking Studio.

items.title: 5. Adjust the scene and export
items.text:
Scene provides additional scene, camera, and rendering options. Color by Role distinguishes receptor and ligand atoms while keeping heteroatoms colored by element. Clear Scene removes the displayed objects from PyMOL; it does not delete their project records. The command line beneath the canvas accepts PyMOL commands for further adjustments.

Export offers Save displayed complex as PDB... and Save ray-traced PNG.... The image export uses a print-sized rendering at 300 dpi.

For a complementary view of the selected pose's contacts, open 2D Interactions.

items.title: QSAR
items.text: The QSAR tool covers model building, review and prediction. Model building comprises four steps: data selection, train/test splitting, descriptor choice and algorithm selection. The QSAR Analysis view in the top catalog allows users to inspect the model metrics and prediction results.

items.title: Typical workflow
items.text:
1. 01 Data Choose endpoint and task
  2. 02 Split Define training and test sets
  3. 03 Descriptors Choose molecular features
  4. 04 Methods Select algorithms and train
↳QSAR AnalysisReview model metrics

After reviewing a model, use QSAR → Predict to score ligands and inspect their predictions in QSAR Analysis → Result analysis.

items.title: 0. Import ligands and activities
items.text:
Before building a model, import the molecular structures and their measured activities through the Ligands catalog. For a CSV, include a SMILES column and one or more numeric/categorical activity columns, with each row containing a compound and its measurements.

For example, a CSV can use the following layout. These five entries are from the MoleculeNet BACE dataset:

smiles name pIC50 BACE_Class n1ccc2c(cccc2)c1N BACE_202 3 0 n1c2c(ccc1N)cccc2 BACE_203 3 0 O=C1NC(=NC(=C1)CCC)N BACE_205 2.6989701 0 O=C(NC1CCCCC1)CCc1cc2cc(ccc2nc1N)-c1ccccc1C BACE_89 7.1307683 1 Fc1ccc(NC(=O)c2ncc(cc2)C#N)cc1[C@]1(N=C(OCC1)N)C BACE_78 7.2923999 1

Here, smiles supplies the molecular structure and name identifies the compound. pIC50 is a continuous endpoint for regression; BACE_Class contains binary labels for classification (0 = inactive, 1 = active). Your file can contain either or both endpoint types, using column names that describe your measurements. Save the data as a CSV with a header row, and select the activity columns during import as described below.

  1. Open Ligands → Import..., select Add files, and choose the input file.

  2. Tick As Reference for each file containing activity measurements. This enables the Activity tab below the file table and allows its measurements to be imported. Reference compounds are stored as project rows, even when screening-library sharding is enabled. Include both active and inactive compounds; the reference mark does not indicate an activity class.

  3. Activity should open automatically when the user ticks as Reference. Under Activity columns (auto-detected from the CSV), tick the columns to import as endpoints. For example, select pIC50 (continuous) for regression and BACE_Class (categorical) for binary classification. The detected columns are unchecked by default; tick the required measurements explicitly and leave unrelated numeric columns unchecked.

  4. When using the detected-column checkboxes, leave Activity from file tag/column blank. For values already expressed as pIC50, leave the transform at (none); do not convert them again or assign concentration units such as nM. To import a single SDF property or table column instead, enter its name under Activity from file tag/column and configure its endpoint, unit and transform as needed.

  5. Select Import and follow progress in the Jobs monitor. Once the job finishes, open Activity from the top toolbar and check that the endpoints and measurements are present.

    As Reference and activity columns are both required

    For a CSV imported through the column checkboxes, marking the file As Reference enables activity import, but does not select any columns. Without selecting the activity columns, the molecules can be imported without the measurements needed to train a model.

See Ligands for more detail on activity import. Once the data are available, open QSAR → Build to follow the four model setup steps below.

items.title: 1. Choose data
items.text: In Data, choose the activity endpoint (target variable) and set the task to regression or classification. A continuous endpoint can be converted to classes with a threshold; categorical endpoint labels are used directly.

items.title: 2. Split the data
items.text: In Split, choose a holdout test fraction and a splitting method. The available methods include random, stratified, scaffold, Butina and MaxMin splits. Use Preview split distribution to inspect the train and test distribution before training.

items.title: 3. Choose descriptors
items.text: In Descriptors, choose RDKit 2D descriptors or ECFP4 fingerprints. RDKit descriptors can be pruned by a correlation cutoff; ECFP4 exposes the fingerprint radius and bit count. Missing features are calculated as part of the training jobs.

items.title: 4. Select methods and train
items.text:
In Methods, select one or more supported algorithms to compare, then set cross-validation folds and optional y-scramble runs. Select Train to submit the model job.

Training jobs appear in the Jobs monitor. After submission, AMDockVS opens QSAR Analysis → Model analysis, where the models become available as training completes.

items.title: Analyze models
items.text:
Model analysis lists trained models and summarizes their task, algorithm, feature type, endpoint, split and reported metrics. Select a model to review its training, holdout-test and cross-validation results. Depending on task and model type, the analysis tools include observed-versus-predicted plots, ROC analysis, feature importance and applicability-domain checks. Selecting a molecule in the model’s analyzed subset links it to the corresponding point in the chart.

Observed vs. PredictedFeature importanceApplicability domain

items.title: Predict
items.text:
Under construction

The QSAR prediction workflow is under construction. The following description is a placeholder for the final workflow.

In QSAR → Predict, tick one or more saved models and choose how to score the project’s ligands. Predict all ligands submits prediction jobs for the selected models. For a screening library stored as shards, use Predict shards; scores remain associated with the shards until you choose Promote top... to add the best-scoring molecules from one model as ligand rows.

After prediction, the application opens QSAR Analysis → Result analysis for that model. Predictions can be reviewed in the results table and filtered by selecting a top N or a value cutoff. Use as selection applies the kept ligands as the global ligand selection. Exclude the rest marks the other scored ligands as excluded; they remain in the project and can be recovered through Filter.

Result analysis shows a selected model’s predictions, confidence and applicability-domain similarity for scored ligands. Selecting a row can highlight that molecule in the 3D viewer when the model uses ECFP4 fingerprints. The applicability-domain value is the mean Tanimoto similarity to the model’s nearest training molecules; a low value flags a prediction as outside the configured domain threshold.

The programmatic interface for endpoints, model training and prediction is documented in the QSAR section of the API guide.

items.title: Receptors
items.text: The Receptors catalog lists the protein structures in the active project. Select Import Receptors... in that catalog, or choose File → Import Receptors..., to open the receptor import panel. This guide describes the panel’s input actions, per-structure review table and import options.

items.title: Add receptor structures
items.text:
The toolbar beside the table provides these actions:

  • Add files — Choose one or more receptor structure files.
  • Add folder — Add supported files from a folder and its subfolders.
  • Add sequence — Paste FASTA or a bare amino-acid sequence. Use : to separate chains. Each FASTA record becomes a sequence input; it has no 3D coordinates until a structure is generated.
  • Download — Fetch structures or sequences by identifier from RCSB PDB (mmCIF), AlphaFold DB, ESM Metagenomic Atlas or UniProt. The dialog accepts PDB IDs, UniProt accessions or MGnify protein IDs, depending on the source.
  • Remove — Remove selected rows from the pending import list. This does not remove receptors already imported into the project.

You can also drop receptor files into the table. While the preview scan is running, the add and remove controls are disabled. Structural preview is available for PDB, mmCIF and PDBQT files. FASTA files can also be selected as sequence inputs; they have no 3D coordinates until a structure is generated.

For downloaded files, Keep the downloaded files reuses them on a later import. Otherwise, files are temporary and are deleted after the import job finishes. The keep option is available when a project is open; temporary files for that project can be reviewed in Settings → Downloads.

items.title: Review each structure
items.text:
After adding files, the panel scans them and shows one row per structure. The preview table lets you make selections separately for each file:

Column What it controls File The selected file name. Downloaded files can be marked temporary. Unit Choose the asymmetric unit or one of the biological assemblies found in the structure. Chains Choose which chains to keep from the selected unit. By default, all available chains are kept. Ligands Choose co-crystal ligands to retain as reference ligands. With no narrower selection, all detected candidates are retained. Metals Choose which detected metal components to keep in the receptor. Waters Choose structural waters to retain. Non-structural waters are controlled by the global option below. As Ligand Also import this receptor as a general ligand, for cases such as docking a protein dimer.

Changing the unit or selected chains updates the available ligand, metal and water choices to match the parts of the structure that remain in scope.

items.title: Set import options
items.text:
The controls below the table apply to the import:

  • Remove non-structural waters — Checked by default. Removes waters not classified as structural; structural waters are selected per file in the Waters column.
  • Grid Box from ligands and coordinated metals — Checked by default. Creates binding-site boxes from the selected co-crystal reference ligands and configured coordinated metals. Turn it off to skip creating boxes during import.
  • Grid Box (Å) — Set the side length of boxes created from the selected ligands or metals. The control accepts 8-40 Å in 1 Å steps; its initial value comes from the docking box-size setting.
  • Metals — Select, add or reorder the coordinated metal types that can define grid-box centers. This global list is separate from the per-file Metals column, which controls whether detected metal components are retained in the receptor.
  • Resolve AltLoc to A / highest occupancy — Checked by default. Resolves alternate atom locations by preferring location A, or the highest occupancy when A is unavailable.
  • Remove cofactors during preparation — Off by default. Cofactors are removed during receptor preparation, not by this import option immediately.

items.title: Start the import
items.text:
Wait for the preview scan to finish, review the selections and options, then select Import. The button becomes available after at least one file has been added and any required preview scan is complete. For files within the preview limit, the scan progress appears in the dialog footer. After submission, follow the import job in the Jobs monitor; the Receptors catalog opens as the job is queued.

For batches larger than 50 files, per-file preview is disabled. The table then shows file format and path instead of the per-structure selection columns, and the import job handles the files without preview-derived binding-site boxes.

items.title: API guide
items.text: Use AMDockVSRuntime as the public facade. A runtime owns the active MolSuite project and its executors, so close it with shutdown() when the work is done.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
Create or open a project, then use the runtime's domain namespaces for your workflow:

from amdockvs import AMDockVSRuntime

runtime = AMDockVSRuntime()
try:
    project = runtime.create_or_open_project(
        name="screening",
        folder="./screening-project",
    )
    print(project)
finally:
    runtime.shutdown()
Namespace Responsibility runtime.loader Ligand and receptor import runtime.molecules Queries, scopes, filters, and saved sets runtime.chemistry Ligand and receptor preparation runtime.complexes Explicit receptor-ligand relationships runtime.qsar Activities, descriptors, models, and predictions runtime.binding_sites Manual sites and P2Rank predictions runtime.docking Preparation, grids, docking with Vina, QuickVina 2, gnina, AutoDock-GPU or Uni-Dock, and results runtime.diversity Clustering and representative selection runtime.tools External tools: status, install, repair

items.title: Projects and jobs
items.text:
runtime = AMDockVSRuntime()
runtime.create_or_open_project(name="demo", folder="./demo-project")

jobs = runtime.loader.load_ligands(["ligands.sdf"])
statuses = runtime.watch_jobs(jobs)

for status in statuses.values():
    print(status.job_id, status.status)

Long operations submit MolSuite jobs. They return a job identifier, or a list of identifiers for partitioned imports. watch_job() and watch_jobs() show a tqdm progress bar in a terminal or notebook; wait_for_job() and wait_for_jobs() wait without one. A job that reads what another one writes waits for it, so a pipeline can be submitted at once and waited for at the end.

items.title: Where jobs run
items.text:
Every job method takes executor_name:

  • Left out, the job goes to the first active executor that can run it: the pool of processes of this machine unless another one was made the default.
  • "thread" runs it on threads of this process, which suits small jobs.
  • The name of an active executor sends it there.
print(runtime.run_destinations())          # [(name, label), ...] active now

job_id = runtime.docking.run(ligands=ligands, receptors=receptors, executor_name="lab-ray")
runtime.resume_job(job_id, "local")        # stop it there and continue it here

Hosts and executors are kept by MolSuite and edited from the Hosts and Executors pages of Settings, or through runtime.workspace (save_host, save_executor, activate): see the ms_flow guide. resume_job() also continues a job that was interrupted or canceled, without running again what it had done.

items.title: Query molecules without loading everything
items.text:
select() returns a lazy Selection[MoleculeRecord]; its .scope is the serializable MoleculeScope used by jobs. A selection can be iterated, counted, streamed, or saved as a stable set.

ligands = runtime.molecules.select(
    role="ligand",
    excluded=False,
)

print(ligands.count())
for molecule in ligands:
    print(molecule.id, molecule.name)

training_set = runtime.molecules.create_set(ligands, name="training ligands")

Pass scopes to downstream APIs when the operation should follow a live query; pass a MoleculeSetRef when reproducibility requires a saved snapshot.

items.title: Chemistry and QSAR
items.text:
Chemistry operations are optional and composable:

job_id = runtime.chemistry.run_ligand_pipeline(
    ["standardize", "protonate", "generate_3d"],
    ligands=ligands,
)
runtime.wait_for_job(job_id)

descriptor_job = runtime.qsar.compute_descriptors(molecule_set=ligands)
runtime.wait_for_job(descriptor_job)

Activities can be assigned directly or loaded from tabular data. Training and prediction consume molecule scopes or saved set references, and training needs at least two ligands with the activity:

runtime.qsar.set_activity(
    ligand_id=42,
    endpoint="IC50",
    value=25.0,
    unit="nM",
    source="assay-1",
)

model = runtime.qsar.train(
    molecule_set=training_set,
    endpoint="IC50",
    algorithm="random_forest",
)
predictions = runtime.qsar.predict(model=int(model.id), molecule_set=ligands)

Both run as jobs and wait for them. Training computes the features a molecule lacks first, in a descriptor job. Training the same model on the same data again returns the stored model. To queue the work without waiting, use submit_train and submit_predict. submit_train takes several algorithms, one task per model:

request = runtime.qsar.submit_train(
    endpoint="IC50",
    algorithm=["ridge", "random_forest"],
    feature_source="ecfp4",
)
runtime.wait_for_jobs([j for j in (request["descriptor_job_id"], request["job_id"]) if j])
# request["existing"] lists the algorithms whose model was already stored

Consult the generated reference for the complete signatures because available model options and return values are defined by the current implementation.

items.title: Binding sites
items.text:
A binding site is a box on a receptor, drawn by hand or predicted:

receptors = runtime.molecules.select(role="receptor")
receptor = receptors.one()

runtime.binding_sites.save_site(
    molecule_id=int(receptor.id),
    name="active site",
    center=(12.0, 13.0, 10.0),
    size=(20.0, 20.0, 20.0),
)

P2Rank predicts them once it is installed through the tools facade:

status = runtime.tools.install("p2rank")

job_id = runtime.binding_sites.predict(receptor_ids=[int(receptor.id)])
runtime.watch_job(job_id)
sites = runtime.binding_sites.select(molecule_id=int(receptor.id), source="p2rank")

runtime.tools.status() lists every managed tool and whether it is ready.

items.title: Docking
items.text:
A docking run needs prepared molecules and a grid on each receptor:

runtime.watch_jobs([
    runtime.docking.prepare_ligands(ligands=ligands),
    runtime.docking.prepare_receptors(receptors=receptors),
])
runtime.docking.set_grid(
    receptor_id=int(receptor.id),
    center=(12.0, 13.0, 10.0),
    size=(20.0, 20.0, 20.0),
)

job_id = runtime.docking.run(ligands=ligands, receptors=receptors, exhaustiveness=8)
runtime.watch_job(job_id)
print(runtime.docking.result_stats())

program chooses the engine: vina (the default), qvina (QuickVina 2), gnina, adgpu (AutoDock-GPU) or unidock (Uni-Dock). The options of any engine go in engine_config, which is validated against that engine's model; for engines other than vina the keyword arguments exhaustiveness, num_modes and vina_cpu are not read.

job_id = runtime.docking.run(
    program="gnina",
    ligands=ligands,
    receptors=receptors,
    engine_config={"exhaustiveness": 8, "num_modes": 9, "scoring_function": "rescore"},
)
Program engine_config keys vina exhaustiveness, num_modes, scoring_function (vina, vinardo, ad4), vina_cpu, ... qvina exhaustiveness, num_modes, vina_cpu, energy_range, seed gnina exhaustiveness, num_modes, vina_cpu, scoring_function (rescore, none, refinement, all), seed adgpu nrun, num_modes, parameter_file, derived_types, seed unidock scoring_function (vina, vinardo), search_mode (fast, balance, detail), num_modes, energy_range, seed

runtime.docking.list_programs() describes them. A pair already docked with the same protocol is skipped unless skip_existing=False.

items.title: Complexes
items.text:
A complex names a receptor-ligand pair explicitly, for redocking or rescoring a known pose:

complex_record = runtime.complexes.create(
    receptor_molecule_id=int(receptor.id),
    ligand_molecule_id=42,
    purpose="redocking",
)
print(runtime.complexes.count(purpose="redocking"))

items.title: Diversity
items.text:
Clustering runs once as a job; choosing what represents each cluster is a separate step that can be repeated on the stored run:

job_id = runtime.diversity.cluster_job(method="bitbirch", threshold=0.65)
runtime.watch_job(job_id)

run = runtime.diversity.list_runs()[0]
runtime.diversity.pick_representatives(run["cluster_run_id"], mode="medoid")
representatives = runtime.diversity.save_centroids_as_set(run["cluster_run_id"], name="diverse")

runtime.diversity.supported_methods() and representative_modes() list the choices.

items.title: Cleanup
items.text:
Always release executors and project resources:

runtime.shutdown()

For scripts, a try/finally block is the safest pattern.

items.title: Pregunta
items.text: ¿Cuesta más correr un cribado con la API de AMDockVS que con un script propio que haga lo mismo "a mano"? Se midieron tiempo, CPU, RAM, disco y archivos, y se compararon los resultados.
path: AMDockVS vs. un script clásico (estilo AMDock 1.x) — 2026-10-18

items.title: Caso de estudio
items.text:
• Ligandos: 500 moléculas de data/Enamine_D10k/Enamine_D10k.sdf (una de cada 20, en orden).
  • Receptor: data/docking/1iep_receptor.pdbqt (ya preparado), caja conocida centro (15.190, 53.903, 16.917), tamaño 20 × 20 × 20 Å.
  • Química (igual en ambos): Dimorphite-DL a pH 7,4 → ETKDGv3 (seed 0xF00D) → meeko 0.8.0 → QuickVina 2.1 con exhaustiveness 8, 9 modos, --cpu 1, seed 0.
  • Máquina: Ryzen 7 3700X (8 núcleos / 16 hilos), 46 GB RAM, NVMe ext4. Ambas corridas limitadas a 14 CPUs (taskset -c 0-13), una detrás de otra, nunca a la vez.
  • Software: main de AMDockVS, ms_flow, ms_components, ms_contactmap y ms_env, entorno MSDD_312.
path: AMDockVS vs. un script clásico (estilo AMDock 1.x) — 2026-10-18

items.title: Qué hace cada lado
items.text:
Script clásico (classic.py): lee el SDF; con multiprocessing.Pool(14), cada worker protona y genera el 3D en proceso, escribe un .sdf, llama a mk_prepare_ligand.py como subproceso y luego a qvina2.1 como subproceso, y lee el mejor score del _out.pdbqt.

AMDockVS (amdockvs_run.py): la API pública con la configuración por defecto. loader.load_ligands / load_receptors → chemistry.run_ligand_pipeline(["protonate", "generate_3d"]) → docking.prepare_ligands(program="qvina") → docking.set_grid → docking.run(program="qvina", engine_config={...}). Corre con un HOME temporal, así que no registra nada en ~/.molsuite.

Medición (measure.py): cada corrida se lanza en un scope cgroup propio (systemd-run --user --scope) con taskset:

Métrica Cómo se obtuvo CPU cpu.stat del cgroup: todo el árbol, subprocesos incluidos RAM Suma del PSS (y del RSS) de todo el árbol, muestreada cada 0,5 s; además memory.peak del cgroup Disco Tamaño real y ocupado de lo que queda en la carpeta de salida

La comparación de scores está en compare_scores.py. Los scores de AMDockVS se leyeron de project.db emparejando por source_index.

items.title: Ajustes que necesitó el script clásico
items.text:
El script ingenuo falló antes de dar resultados válidos. En los dos casos AMDockVS ya trae la solución por defecto:

  1. Anillos de 7 o más átomos: meeko, por defecto, los marca como flexibles y escribe los tipos CG0/G0, que QuickVina rechaza ("CG0" is not a valid AutoDock type). Se añadió --rigid_macrocycles.
  2. Sales (.Cl, .Br): meeko rechaza moléculas de varios fragmentos. Esto no se corrigió en el script, para dejar constancia del fallo, así que esos 2 ligandos (Z3072634657, Z2568340255) no se docaron. AMDockVS se queda con el fragmento orgánico mayor y sí los docó (−8,2 y −7,8 kcal/mol).

Los resultados son idénticos: los 498 ligandos comunes tienen exactamente el mismo mejor score en los dos lados (Pearson = Spearman = 1,0).

No se pudo medir la escritura a disco. El cgroup de usuario no tiene el controlador io, y el delta de /proc/diskstats mide todo el dispositivo: dio ~330 MB en las dos corridas, casi todo de otros procesos. Se descartó.

items.title: Por qué salen así
items.text:
• El tiempo empata porque manda QuickVina: ~36 s por ligando, el 99 % del total. Dos efectos de signo contrario se compensan:
  • El script arranca un Python con meeko por cada ligando: 1,35 s de pared, 3,5 s de CPU y 258 MB por llamada. Esos ~1750 s de CPU explican la mayor parte de su exceso de CPU y los picos de RAM.
  • AMDockVS pierde ~45 s al final porque agrupa 4 ligandos por chunk de docking. En los últimos ~100 s quedan CPUs paradas, pero eso solo explica ~4 puntos del uso medio.
  • El uso medio (98 % vs 81 %) no mide eficiencia. En las dos corridas QuickVina usa ~0,85 s de CPU por segundo de pared: 14 827 s de CPU entre ~17 400 s de slots ocupados en AMDockVS. El 98 % del script no viene de docar mejor: son ~3000 s de CPU extra (arrancar Python y meeko por ligando) que ocupan las CPUs al mismo tiempo que el docking.
  • Tamaño del batch de docking. Se simuló el reparto con las 498 duraciones reales:
Ligandos por chunk Tiempo total simulado 1 1299 s 2 1317 s 4 (por defecto) 1345 s 8 1437 s Ideal (sin cola) 1275 s

Con 500 ligandos, pasar de 4 a 1 ahorraría ~3,5 %; con 5000, menos del 0,5 %. No justifica cambiarlo, salvo quizás usar chunks más pequeños cuando hay pocos pares por CPU. - RAM. QuickVina corre desde hilos del proceso principal, sin un worker de Python por cada run, y meeko se importa una sola vez. El script tiene 14 workers con RDKit, más hasta 14 meeko arrancando a la vez.
